Your guess: What does a “typical” wait look like? Is there one typical wait time, or more than one? Scroll through the table and decide before opening the chart.

TipReveal the histogram
Show the Python code 
fig, ax = plt.subplots()
sns.histplot(data=waits, x="wait_minutes", binwidth=1, color="#2a6f97", ax=ax)
ax.axvline(waits["wait_minutes"].mean(), color="#d1495b", ls="--", lw=2)
ax.annotate(f"mean = {waits['wait_minutes'].mean():.1f} min",
            xy=(waits["wait_minutes"].mean(), ax.get_ylim()[1] * 0.9),
            xytext=(8, 0), textcoords="offset points", color="#d1495b")
ax.set(xlabel="Wait time (minutes)", ylabel="Number of customers",
       title="Two humps: there are two kinds of customers")
plt.show()

There are two typical waits: about 4 minutes and about 17 minutes. (In the simulation these are chat vs. phone customers.) Notice the mean, about 10 minutes, describes almost nobody. A single summary number hid the most important fact, and so did the table.

NoteData format for the histogram

A histogram needs one numeric column with one row per observation (here, one row per customer, 240 rows). Leave the values raw: don’t bin or count them yourself, because sns.histplot() sorts the values into bins and counts how many land in each.

Column Type Role in the chart
wait_minutes numeric (decimal minutes) x: the values that get binned and counted
ticket_id integer ID not used; it just identifies each row

Row order doesn’t matter, and any missing values in wait_minutes are simply left out.

TipReveal the pie chart
Show the Python code 
counts = tickets["category"].value_counts()
colors = sns.color_palette("Set2", len(counts))

fig, ax = plt.subplots(figsize=(6.5, 6.5))
ax.pie(counts.values, labels=counts.index, colors=colors, autopct="%1.0f%%",

plt.show()

Billing alone is close to half of all tickets. In the table, “Billing” just looks like one word that comes up “a lot.”

NoteData format for the pie chart

A pie chart needs one number per category: the size of each slice. The categories must be mutually exclusive (each ticket falls in exactly one) and together make up a meaningful whole (all tickets).

The export arrives as one row per ticket (200 rows), so it has to be counted up first:

Column Type Role in the chart
category text (categorical) defines the slices; every ticket has exactly one category
ticket_id, date, priority ID, date, text not used by this chart

tickets["category"].value_counts() turns that into counts, a pandas Series with one entry per category (5 entries), sorted largest to smallest:

Index (label) Value
each category name, e.g. Billing number of tickets in that category

ax.pie() then takes counts.values as the slice sizes and counts.index as the labels. Because the counts are sorted, explode=[0.06] + [0] * ... pulls out the first (largest) slice. If your spreadsheet already has a summary table, with one row per category and a count column, you can skip value_counts() and pass those two columns straight to ax.pie(). The sorted bar chart in the note below uses the same counts.

NoteA note on pie charts

Pie charts work when you have a few categories that add up to a meaningful whole and one or two slices matter most, like here. Humans judge angles poorly, so with many similar-sized slices, a sorted bar chart is usually easier to read:

Show the Python code 
fig, ax = plt.subplots()
sns.barplot(x=counts.values / counts.sum() * 100, y=counts.index, color="#2a6f97", ax=ax)
ax.set(xlabel="Percent of tickets", ylabel="", title="Same data as a sorted bar chart")
plt.show()

title: "Histograms & Pie Charts"
subtitle: "The shape of one variable, and parts of a whole"

```{python}
#| echo: false
import pandas as pd
import matplotlib.pyplot as plt
import seaborn as sns
from sim_data import wait_times, ticket_categories

pd.set_option("display.max_rows", 500)
sns.set_theme(style="whitegrid", font_scale=1.05)
```

## Experiment 1: Customer wait times

A support center logged how many minutes each of 240 customers waited before talking to someone.

::: {.raw-table}
```{python}
#| code-fold: true
waits = wait_times()
waits
```
:::

::: {.guess}
**Your guess:** What does a "typical" wait look like? Is there one typical wait time, or more than one? Scroll through the table and decide before opening the chart.
:::

::: {.callout-tip collapse="true"}
## Reveal the histogram

```{python}
fig, ax = plt.subplots()
sns.histplot(data=waits, x="wait_minutes", binwidth=1, color="#2a6f97", ax=ax)
ax.axvline(waits["wait_minutes"].mean(), color="#d1495b", ls="--", lw=2)
ax.annotate(f"mean = {waits['wait_minutes'].mean():.1f} min",
            xy=(waits["wait_minutes"].mean(), ax.get_ylim()[1] * 0.9),
            xytext=(8, 0), textcoords="offset points", color="#d1495b")
ax.set(xlabel="Wait time (minutes)", ylabel="Number of customers",
       title="Two humps: there are two kinds of customers")
plt.show()
```

[There are **two** typical waits: about 4 minutes and about 17 minutes. (In the simulation these are chat vs. phone customers.) Notice the mean, about 10 minutes, describes almost *nobody*. A single summary number hid the most important fact, and so did the table.]{.reveal-note}
:::

::: {.callout-note collapse="true"}
## Data format for the histogram
A histogram needs **one numeric column** with **one row per observation** (here, one row per customer, 240 rows). Leave the values raw: don't bin or count them yourself, because `sns.histplot()` sorts the values into bins and counts how many land in each.

| Column | Type | Role in the chart |
|---|---|---|
| `wait_minutes` | numeric (decimal minutes) | `x`: the values that get binned and counted |
| `ticket_id` | integer ID | not used; it just identifies each row |

Row order doesn't matter, and any missing values in `wait_minutes` are simply left out.
:::

## Experiment 2: What are people contacting us about?

Here are 200 support tickets from September, sorted by date, the way a ticketing system exports them.

::: {.raw-table}
```{python}
tickets = ticket_categories()
tickets
```
:::

::: {.guess}
**Your guess:** Roughly what share of tickets is about each category? Is one category dominating, or are they spread evenly?
:::

::: {.callout-tip collapse="true"}
## Reveal the pie chart

```{python}
counts = tickets["category"].value_counts()
colors = sns.color_palette("Set2", len(counts))

fig, ax = plt.subplots(figsize=(6.5, 6.5))
ax.pie(counts.values, labels=counts.index, colors=colors, autopct="%1.0f%%",
       startangle=90, counterclock=False, explode=[0.06] + [0] * (len(counts) - 1),
       wedgeprops={"edgecolor": "white", "linewidth": 2}, textprops={"fontsize": 11})
ax.set_title("Nearly half of all tickets are about billing")
plt.show()
```

[Billing alone is close to half of all tickets. In the table, "Billing" just looks like one word that comes up "a lot."]{.reveal-note}
:::

::: {.callout-note collapse="true"}
## Data format for the pie chart
A pie chart needs **one number per category**: the size of each slice. The categories must be **mutually exclusive** (each ticket falls in exactly one) and together make up a **meaningful whole** (all tickets).

The export arrives as **one row per ticket** (200 rows), so it has to be counted up first:

| Column | Type | Role in the chart |
|---|---|---|
| `category` | text (categorical) | defines the slices; every ticket has exactly one category |
| `ticket_id`, `date`, `priority` | ID, date, text | not used by this chart |

`tickets["category"].value_counts()` turns that into `counts`, a pandas Series with **one entry per category** (5 entries), sorted largest to smallest:

| Index (label) | Value |
|---|---|
| each category name, e.g. `Billing` | number of tickets in that category |

`ax.pie()` then takes `counts.values` as the slice sizes and `counts.index` as the labels. Because the counts are sorted, `explode=[0.06] + [0] * ...` pulls out the first (largest) slice. If your spreadsheet already has a summary table, with one row per category and a count column, you can skip `value_counts()` and pass those two columns straight to `ax.pie()`. The sorted bar chart in the note below uses the same `counts`.
:::

::: {.callout-note collapse="true"}
## A note on pie charts
Pie charts work when you have **a few categories** that **add up to a meaningful whole** and one or two slices matter most, like here. Humans judge angles poorly, so with many similar-sized slices, a sorted bar chart is usually easier to read:

```{python}
#| fig-height: 3.5
fig, ax = plt.subplots()
sns.barplot(x=counts.values / counts.sum() * 100, y=counts.index, color="#2a6f97", ax=ax)
ax.set(xlabel="Percent of tickets", ylabel="", title="Same data as a sorted bar chart")
plt.show()
```
:::
 

Built with Quarto, pandas, matplotlib, and seaborn. All data are simulated.
